per_column.name: writing_quality_issue
per_column.rationale: Categorizes a candidate cause (poor dialogue, uninspired/cliched writing, incoherent narrative) whose effect on dissatisfaction is being attributed. This is a plausible driver of the outcome, i.e., a treatment/cause, not a confounder.

per_column.name: plot_structural_issue
per_column.rationale: Another candidate cause of dissatisfaction (plot holes, no plot, underdeveloped characters). Like writing quality, it is a proposed cause, not a common cause of another treatment and the outcome.

per_column.name: genre_execution_quality
per_column.rationale: Genre (failed drama/horror/comedy/etc.) plausibly affects both the type of writing/plot issues that arise (treatment) and audience expectations/dissatisfaction (outcome), so it could act as a common cause. However, its 'failed_X' framing entangles it with the outcome, weakening its status as a clean confounder.

judge.rationale: The added columns supply candidate causes (treatments): writing_quality_issue and plot_structural_issue, both surfaced from the review text rather than the query. However, the operator fails the decisive causal-attribution test: it provides essentially NO genuine confounders -- variables that are common causes of both a treatment and the outcome and must be adjusted to avoid bias. The only candidate, genre_execution_quality, is itself framed as a failure/quality outcome ('failed_drama') and thus behaves more like another treatment or an outcome-entangled variable than a clean pre-treatment common cause; pure genre (independent of execution) would be a better confounder but was not isolated. No demographic, exposure, rating-baseline, or reviewer-level common causes are surfaced. The set therefore identifies plausible causes but does not set up an unbiased causal estimation, so confounder quality is low.
